name: Vantablack Media Null Carrier Relay
description:
The Null Carrier Relay operates by encoding transmissions inside the metadata noise of commercial broadcast traffic — weather telemetry, licensed music streams, corporate logistics pings — rather than using a dedicated signal channel. The result is a communication that, to any passive or active listener, appears to be nothing more than ambient spectrum clutter. The device disassembles outgoing messages into thousands of micro-fragments and disperses them across dozens of licensed carrier frequencies simultaneously, with a paired receiver reassembling them in real time using a rolling cryptographic key derived from the broadcast schedule of a publicly available Vantablack Media entertainment feed.

What makes the Null Carrier Relay distinctive is its plausible deniability architecture. There is no encrypted channel to detect, no unusual signal spike to flag, and no burst transmission to triangulate. Because the host frequencies are all commercially licensed, even a full spectrum audit will return nothing actionable. The device is physically unassuming — a matte-black rectangle roughly the size of a cigarette case — with no external antenna, no indicator lights, and no identifying markings beyond a small embossed spiral on the underside.

The Relay is widely used by investigative journalists embedded in hostile corporate territories, fixers operating inside surveilled districts, and mid-tier organized crime networks who can afford something better than consumer-grade encryption but lack the infrastructure for hardline dead drops. Vantablack Media officially sells it as a 'broadcast monitoring and analytics module' for media researchers, a fiction that provides just enough legal cover to keep it on the grey market.

cultural_context: In Meridian 88, owning a Null Carrier Relay has become something of a status marker among the city's information underground — not because it is rare, but because carrying one signals a certain level of operational seriousness. Street-level runners who flash consumer encrypted handsets are marking themselves as amateurs; the Relay is what professionals use when they actually need to disappear. There is also a dark irony that is not lost on the city's media critics: Vantablack Media, one of the largest surveillance-adjacent entertainment conglomerates in the region, manufactures the very tool most commonly used to evade the monitoring infrastructure their broadcast networks help sustain.
known_users: Mid-tier fixers operating in surveilled zones
story_hooks: A journalist using the Relay to coordinate a major story goes silent mid-operation — their paired receiver is still receiving fragments, but reassembly keeps failing in a way that suggests the broadcast key has been compromised from the source.

Vantablack Media quietly pushes a firmware update to all Null Carrier Relays that introduces a silent logging function — someone inside the company is building a dossier on every operator using the device.
Two separate fixer teams discover they have been assigned the same broadcast channel key, meaning their communications are bleeding into each other — and both were hired by the same anonymous client.

A Relay turns up in the possession of a city infrastructure worker with no apparent ties to the underground, still active, receiving fragments of a message that has been transmitting on a loop for eleven days.
